passage:
The research institute in Dehradun was quiet in the week between Christmas and New Year, and Eshaan had one important task: email Dr Rawat that the October survey data had a coding error and the report would be two weeks late.
It was a four-line email. He drafted it on Monday. On Tuesday he reorganised his desk drawers. On Wednesday he answered forty unimportant messages and felt busy. Every time he opened the draft, his chest tightened, and he pictured Dr Rawat's cold reply, the meeting, the look.
On Thursday Jahnavi, from the next cubicle, saw the draft on his screen. "Still that one?"
"It's four lines," Eshaan said. "I know. I just can't make myself send it."
"What's the worst he'll say?"
"That I'm careless."
"And if he hears it on 2 January instead?"
Eshaan sat very still, then clicked send before he could think again. His hands were cold.

qa.q: What did Eshaan need to tell Dr Rawat?
qa.a: That the October survey data had a coding error and the report would be two weeks late.

qa.q: Why did a four-line email feel so hard for Eshaan?
qa.a: Eshaan dreaded Dr Rawat's reaction, the cold reply and being seen as careless, so the small task carried a large feeling of fear and shame.

qa.q: What helped Eshaan send it, and what could help next time?
qa.a: Jahnavi's questions made the cost of waiting clear; next time Eshaan could name the fear, set a fixed time to send, or read the draft to a colleague and send straight after.

qa.q: How might Dr Rawat feel getting the news on Thursday rather than on 2 January?
qa.a: Dr Rawat would probably be less annoyed hearing it early, with time to plan, than learning of it late after the holidays.

grounding: An adult puts off a short but important email for days because he dreads the reply; the task is small but the feeling is large.

passage:
Dolma had promised the tea co-operative in Kalimpong a new price list by the first of the month. It was the ninth. Every morning she opened the file, felt a wave of "You're useless, you always do this," and closed it again.
On Saturday, walking back from the market with Trisha, she said it out loud. "I'm so lazy. I hate myself for this."
Trisha stopped by the prayer flags. "You've been running your mother's shop and doing your job all month. You're tired, not lazy. What if you forgive yourself for the nine days and do five minutes when you get home?"
"Five minutes won't finish it."
"It'll start it."
That evening Dolma set a timer. Five minutes. She told herself: I'm behind, and that's okay, it happens. She typed in the first three prices. When the timer rang she kept going for another forty minutes, and sent the list on Monday.

qa.q: By which date had Dolma promised the price list?
qa.a: By the first of the month.

qa.q: What changed in how Dolma felt when she sat down that evening?
qa.a: Instead of calling herself useless, she felt kinder towards herself ("I'm behind, and that's okay"), which made the file less frightening to open.

qa.q: Why did forgiveness plus five minutes work better than self-blame?
qa.a: Harsh self-talk made her close the file every morning; kindness eased the guilt, five minutes was small enough to start, and starting carried her on for forty minutes.

qa.q: How does Trisha see Dolma's delay?
qa.a: Trisha sees tiredness from juggling her mother's shop and a job, not laziness, and wants Dolma to go easier on herself.

grounding: An adult forgives herself for a delay and commits to five minutes, and the kindness helps her return to the task where self-blame had kept her away.

passage:
At the summer camp in the hills, the younger boys' dormitory had one bedtime routine, and Ayesha Aunty, the house mother, never changed it. At half past eight the bell rang. Brush teeth at the long steel sink. Pyjamas on. Everyone on their beds while Ayesha Aunty read one chapter of the story about the lost elephant. Lights out.
The first night Vaibhav cried for home and lay awake till late. By the fourth night, when the bell rang, he was at the sink before he'd even thought about it. By the end of the week he yawned the moment she opened the book.
On the last night the generator failed and the bell never rang, but at half past eight Vaibhav was brushing his teeth by torchlight.

qa.q: What did Ayesha Aunty read each night?
qa.a: One chapter of the story about the lost elephant.

qa.q: How did Vaibhav feel on the first night compared with the end of the week?
qa.a: On the first night he felt homesick and couldn't sleep; by the end of the week he felt settled and sleepy, yawning as soon as the story began.

qa.q: What made the bedtime steps work so well?
qa.a: The same order at the same time every night, with the bell as the cue, so each step led to the next without anyone having to decide.

qa.q: How might Ayesha Aunty feel seeing Vaibhav brushing by torchlight?
qa.a: She would likely be amused and pleased to see the routine running by itself, even without the bell. 😊

grounding: A child at camp follows the same bedtime steps at the same time each night until they happen automatically, even without the bell.

subtype: Reaching for the phone when bored [Actor]
passage:
"Irawati, you did it again."
"Did what?"
"The phone. I paused the movie to get the sweets, and in the four seconds before I stood up, it was already in your hand."
"I didn't even notice."
"I know. That's the scary part. You did it while the rangoli powder was drying. When Mausi went to answer the door. When the ad came on."
"I'm not even looking for anything. I just... scroll."
"What were you scrolling just now?"
"...I don't know. A video of a dog. Someone's new shoes."
"And?"
"And it's nice for a second. Something new."
"Try this. For the rest of Diwali, your phone goes in my bag when we're together. When you're bored, just tell me you're bored."
"That's embarrassing."
"Try it anyway, Iru."
"Okay, Devika. But you're holding it."

qa.q: What was Irawati scrolling just now?
qa.a: A video of a dog and someone's new shoes.

qa.q: What does "I didn't even notice" suggest about Irawati?
qa.a: Irawati seems startled and a little embarrassed; reaching for the phone has become automatic, set off by each pause rather than chosen.

qa.q: Why might Devika's idea help?
qa.a: Putting the phone in the bag breaks the easy grab, and saying "I'm bored" names the feeling that starts the loop, so Irawati can choose something else.

qa.q: What is it like for Devika to watch this?
qa.a: Devika seems worried, calling it the scary part, and maybe a little lonely, since Irawati drifts to the phone at every pause in their time together.

grounding: A teenager reaches for the phone at every pause and scrolls without deciding, a loop of boredom, scrolling and a small hit of novelty.

passage:
Rukmini sat down beside her son on the sofa.
"Samir, can I show you something? Not a lecture, promise."
"Mm."
"I've been watching this week. You come in, drop your bag, sit on this exact cushion, and the phone's out before your shoes are off. Every day. Then suddenly it's six o'clock."
"...So?"
"So it's not you being lazy. It's the sofa. On Sunday, at the table, you did homework for an hour without looking at your phone once."
"That's because Nana was talking to me."
"Maybe. Or because the table isn't where the phone lives. What if the charger moves to the kitchen, and you have your snack at the table first?"
"And if I want to use it?"
"Then use it, after the snack, for a set time. I'm not taking it. I'm just moving the sofa's magic."
"You're weird, Ammi."
"I know. One week?"
"...Fine. One week."

qa.q: Where does Rukmini suggest moving the charger?
qa.a: To the kitchen.

qa.q: What does Rukmini seem to want when she says "Not a lecture, promise"?
qa.a: Rukmini seems hopeful and careful, wanting Samir to see the pattern himself instead of feeling nagged or blamed.

qa.q: Why is changing the setting smarter than nagging?
qa.a: The habit starts from a cue, the sofa cushion, so moving the charger and starting at the table removes the trigger instead of relying on Samir's willpower every afternoon.

qa.q: How might Samir feel about the plan?
qa.a: Samir seems wary at first, then amused and willing, since the phone isn't being taken away and it's only for a week.

grounding: A mother notices her son's phone habit starts the moment he sits on the sofa and helps him change the setting instead of nagging.

passage:
Tuesday, monsoon, mid-sem week

Tried Kamal's idea tonight: every time I reached for the chips or the phone, write down what happened just before.
9:10: opened circuits notes. Saw problem 4. Stomach dropped. Chips.
9:25: Kamal messaged about the lab report deadline. Heart racing. Scrolled for 20 min.
10:05: rain got loud, remembered I haven't called home. Chips again.
10:40: tried problem 4 again. Phone.
Every single time: something stressed me, I grabbed something, felt better for about a minute, then worse because nothing was done.
So it's not that I love chips. It's that I hate the stomach-drop feeling, and chips make it go away for a minute.
Tomorrow: when problem 4 does the stomach thing, I'll get up, drink water, and write just the first line. Let's see.

Gargi

qa.q: What happened at 9:10?
qa.a: Gargi opened the circuits notes, saw problem 4, the stomach dropped, and it was chips.

qa.q: What feeling is Gargi trying to escape by grabbing chips or the phone?
qa.a: The stomach-drop feeling of stress; the snack or scroll brings about a minute of relief, and then Gargi feels worse because nothing is done.

qa.q: Why is Gargi's plan for tomorrow a good one?
qa.a: Having found the trigger, stress at a hard problem, Gargi swaps the response for water and just the first line, so the need for relief is met without losing the evening.

qa.q: How might Kamal feel reading Gargi's log?
qa.a: Kamal would likely feel glad the idea helped, and maybe a bit sheepish that the 9:25 message set off twenty minutes of scrolling.

grounding: A student logs what happens before each snack or scroll and finds a loop of stress, grabbing and brief relief, which shows where to change it.

passage:
Raghav's call-centre shift in Kochi ran till midnight, and every time a customer shouted at him he did the same thing: muted, grabbed his phone, and scrolled until the next call. By the end of the shift his eyes ached and he felt worse, not better.
He didn't try to ban the phone; he'd tried that and failed. Instead he kept the cue, an angry call, and changed what came after. Angry call ends: stand up, walk to the window at the end of the floor and back, slow breaths on the way. Ninety seconds. The floor was never quiet, but the corridor was enough.
He tracked it on a sticky note: a tick for a walk, a cross for a scroll. First week: nine ticks, six crosses. Second week: fourteen ticks, two crosses.
"You look less fried," Jomon said on Friday.
"Still angry customers," Raghav said. "I just stopped carrying them into my phone."

qa.q: How many ticks and crosses did Raghav get in the second week?
qa.a: Fourteen ticks, two crosses.

qa.q: Why did scrolling feel like a good idea after an angry call?
qa.a: Raghav felt stressed and rattled, and scrolling promised a quick escape, though it left him feeling worse by the end of the shift.

qa.q: Why did swapping in the walk work better than banning the phone?
qa.a: It kept the same cue and still met the need to calm down after an angry call, but with a walk and slow breaths, and the sticky note showed the change working.

qa.q: How does Jomon see the change?
qa.a: Jomon notices Raghav looks "less fried", so from outside the change shows up as a calmer colleague on a noisy shift.

grounding: An adult keeps the cue of an angry call but swaps stress scrolling for a short walk and breathing, and tracks the result.

subtype: Restless and asking what to do [Actor]
passage:
"Papa, I'm bored."
"It's been ten minutes since lunch, Pallavi."
"Can I have the tablet? Please? There's nothing to do."
"No tablet. But here." Omkar put down an empty cardboard box, a roll of tape and some old newspaper.
"That's not a toy."
"Okay." He went back to his book. Monsoon rain drummed on the roof.
Pallavi kicked the box. Then she sat in it. Then she taped newspaper over the top.
Twenty minutes later: "Papa! Don't come in! It's my rain house and you need a ticket!"

qa.q: What did Omkar put down for Pallavi?
qa.a: An empty cardboard box, a roll of tape and some old newspaper.

qa.q: How did Pallavi feel when she kicked the box?
qa.a: She felt restless and grumpy, still bored and cross that there was no tablet.

qa.q: What did Omkar get right?
qa.a: He said no to the screen, offered simple materials and then left her alone with time, so the boredom had room to turn into play.

qa.q: What might Omkar feel when he hears about the ticket?
qa.a: Omkar is probably amused and pleased to see her boredom turn into a game of her own. 😄

grounding: A young child complains of boredom and wants a screen, and simple materials plus time turn the boredom into imaginative play.

subtype: Bored by a class that is too easy or too hard [Actor]
passage:
Thursday, winter, cold enough to write with a shawl on

Maths again. Hansa Ma'am spent the whole period on adding fractions with the same denominator. I did those in Class 5. I finished the worksheet in four minutes, then drew a whole city in the margin with a metro line and a flyover. Then counted the pigeons on the wire outside. Eleven.
She said, "Varun, pay attention, you're always in your own world." Everyone looked. I wasn't being lazy. I was just empty. Like waiting at a bus stop for a bus that isn't coming.
But in physics it's the opposite. I haven't understood anything since the chapter on force, so I stare out of the window there too. Same window, opposite reason.
Maybe I should tell Hansa Ma'am the worksheet takes me four minutes. Maybe she'd give me harder ones.

Varun

qa.q: How long did Varun take to finish the maths worksheet?
qa.a: Four minutes.

qa.q: How does Varun feel during maths?
qa.a: Varun feels bored and empty, like waiting for a bus that isn't coming, and a bit stung at being told to pay attention in front of everyone.

qa.q: What could Varun and Hansa Ma'am do?
qa.a: Varun could tell her the worksheet takes four minutes and ask for harder problems, and in physics ask for help going back to the chapter on force; both are mismatches, not laziness.

qa.q: How might Hansa Ma'am see Varun's doodling?
qa.a: Hansa Ma'am seems to read it as not paying attention, without knowing the work is far too easy for Varun.

grounding: A teenager doodles and stares out of the window because one lesson is far too easy and another too hard, showing boredom as a mismatch, not laziness.
